family_08/archetype_053.archetype_query: First-Wave Punk / 70s Punk: Ramones, Sex Pistols, The Clash, Buzzcocks, The Damned, X-Ray Spex, Wire, X, and the first 1970s punk single/album language.

selected_sources.title: Anarchy in the Archives: Punk Arrives
selected_sources.why_fit: Gives archival New York punk context for Ramones, CBGB, fanzines, DIY circulation, and early scene formation.

selected_sources.title: Ramones
selected_sources.why_fit: Supports Ramones as a concise, fast, minimalist anchor for the archetype.

selected_sources.title: The Clash
selected_sources.why_fit: Supports The Clash as the politicized, stylistically expansive first-wave punk branch.

rejected_sources.title: CBGB: The Unique History
rejected_sources.why_rejected: Useful for CBGB-specific archetype 054, but too narrow as the main source for the broader first-wave punk archetype.

family_08/archetype_053.why_selected_sources_fit: The selected set triangulates a broad reference definition, an archive of New York punk circulation, and two canonical object supports for the Ramones and Clash poles.

claims.claim_text: First-wave punk condensed rock into short songs, blunt hooks, fast tempos, and a visible DIY stance, making Ramones and Sex Pistols useful opposite-shore anchors.
The Clash broadened punk beyond three-chord minimalism by folding reggae, dub, rockabilly, and political journalism into a still-punk frame.
New York punk spread through clubs, zines, record shops, and small labels before it became a mass-media style label.
The archetype should be separated from later pop-punk by its rougher recording feel, sharper anti-establishment posture, and first-generation scene function.

render_seed.short_definition: 1970s punk at its first blast: fast, spare, anti-polished, and scene-built.
render_seed.history_capsule: This road starts with New York minimalism and UK volatility, then branches into melodic, political, and artier versions of the same refusal.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It changed who could plausibly start a band and made small scenes feel historically powerful.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: Short songs, clipped riffs, shouted or sneered vocals, and DIY immediacy matter more than virtuoso rock display.
did_you_know: Early punk was as much a network of venues, flyers, labels, and fanzines as a sound.
The Clash are useful here because they show punk expanding without leaving its first-wave frame.
render_seed.caution: Do not treat every later punk-adjacent pop song as first-wave punk; keep the 1970s scene and recording language in view.

Note: compared with the prior v0.2.1 generic punk claim set, these are stronger for 054; the parent builder may restore the hardened proof pack.

claims.claim_text: CBGB opened on the Bowery in 1973 and became a practical stage where downtown New York punk, art-punk, and early new wave could develop in public.
Television, Patti Smith, Ramones, Talking Heads, and Blondie make the archetype distinct because the same venue supported poetry-rock, minimal punk, nervous funk, and pop-facing new wave.
Patti Smith's Horses is a key example because it joins literary performance, garage-rock attack, and downtown art-world energy rather than just standard rock-band craft.
Talking Heads and Blondie show why this road should not collapse into first-wave punk alone: it also points toward dance rhythm, art-school angularity, and pop/video-era new wave.

render_seed.short_definition: Downtown New York punk as a venue-made ecosystem, not just a guitar style.
render_seed.history_capsule: CBGB turned the Bowery into a testing ground where poets, art students, stripped-down rock bands, and pop experimenters shared a stage.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It proved that a small club could become an international map point for punk, new wave, and art-rock memory.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The sound can be jagged, literary, danceable, minimalist, or pop-smart, held together by downtown scene logic.
did_you_know: CBGB's full name included OMFUG, a phrase that signaled music for unconventional music makers.
The same scene can explain Patti Smith and Talking Heads without pretending they sound identical.
render_seed.caution: Do not use CBGB as a synonym for all punk; keep the downtown art-punk and new-wave crossings visible.

family_08/archetype_055.why_selected_sources_fit: The set moves from punk background to US hardcore-specific labels and canonical examples, avoiding a venue-only family template.

claims.claim_text: US hardcore accelerated punk into shorter, faster, harsher songs, with Black Flag and Minor Threat making speed and discipline central listening clues.
Dischord and SST matter historically because they show hardcore as an independent label and touring network, not just a heavier sound.
Dead Kennedys and Bad Brains widen the archetype through political satire, reggae-informed velocity, and regional scenes beyond Los Angeles and Washington, DC.
Hardcore should be kept separate from first-wave punk by its 1980s all-ages, regional, faster-and-harder infrastructure.

render_seed.short_definition: The 1980s US punk pressure cooker: faster, cheaper, louder, and more self-organized.
render_seed.history_capsule: Hardcore took punk's permission structure and rebuilt it through regional scenes, indie labels, vans, basement shows, and all-ages rooms.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It created the underground logistics that later alternative, emo, post-hardcore, and indie scenes inherited.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: Speed, barked vocals, tight riffs, and anti-commercial infrastructure distinguish it from both first-wave punk and metal.
did_you_know: Hardcore history is also label history: Dischord and SST are part of the sound's architecture.
Straight edge is one hardcore branch, not the whole archetype.
render_seed.caution: Do not read one loud guitar as hardcore; listen for the faster US punk scene grammar.

family_08/archetype_056.archetype_query: Post-Punk / Dark Melodic / Gothic Roots: Joy Division, The Cure, Siouxsie and the Banshees, Bauhaus, Echo and the Bunnymen, dark bass-led 1979-1980s mutation.

rejected_sources.title: Hardcore Punk
rejected_sources.why_rejected: Hardcore explains a neighboring punk intensification, but not the dark melodic and gothic post-punk branch.

family_08/archetype_056.why_selected_sources_fit: The sources support post-punk as a punk afterlife with darker melody and experiment, with The Cure as object evidence and new wave/synthpop as boundary context.

claims.claim_text: Post-punk kept punk's refusal but moved the center toward basslines, negative space, studio atmosphere, and art-school experimentation.
Joy Division and The Cure make the archetype audible through low-register bass movement, austere drums, and melody that feels tense rather than triumphant.
The gothic-roots side of the road is a mood and arrangement language before it is a costume: reverb, minor-key hooks, and theatrical shadow carry the signal.
This archetype borders synthpop and new wave, but it should remain darker, stranger, and less pop-surface-first than the MTV new wave road.

render_seed.short_definition: Punk after midnight: bass-led, atmospheric, melodic, and uneasy.
render_seed.history_capsule: After punk's first blast, some bands slowed the rush down and opened space for dread, dub, art-rock, and gothic melody.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It became a durable source for alternative rock's darker emotional vocabulary.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The drums and bass often carry the architecture while guitars, synths, and voices create weather around them.
did_you_know: Gothic roots here means a musical pathway, not just fashion.
The Cure can sit here even when some songs are bright because the broader road includes dark melodic framing.
render_seed.caution: Do not flatten post-punk into goth only; keep the experimental and rhythmic branches open.

family_08/archetype_057.why_selected_sources_fit: Britannica supplies direct style framing; Rock Hall pages ground the Cars and Police examples; MTV is limited to video-era transmission context.

claims.claim_text: New wave made punk-adjacent brevity and nervous energy compatible with polished choruses, synthesizers, and radio-ready pop-rock.
The Cars anchor this road because their hits balance clipped guitar, synthesizer color, deadpan vocals, and clean studio hooks.
The Police show the archetype's crossover power by mixing punk-era trio economy with reggae rhythm and arena-scale pop choruses.
MTV-era presentation matters for this road because image, video repetition, and concise singles helped turn new wave into mainstream pop language.

render_seed.short_definition: Punk's sharp edges cleaned into bright, stylish, video-era pop-rock.
render_seed.history_capsule: New wave carried some punk economy into the 1980s but made room for synthesizers, reggae/dance rhythm, fashion, and pop hooks.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It helped alternative energy become mainstream without needing classic-rock heaviness.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The signal is clipped and catchy: guitar, synth, image, and chorus all work together.
did_you_know: New wave is a bridge: it can point back to punk or forward to synthpop and MTV pop.
The Police are useful because they show new wave's rhythmic crossover side.
render_seed.caution: Do not overfit all 1980s pop to new wave; listen for punk-era economy and angularity under the polish.

family_08/archetype_058.archetype_query: Synthpop / New Romantic / 80s Electronic Pop: Depeche Mode, New Order, Human League, Pet Shop Boys, Yazoo, Soft Cell, synth hooks and drum-machine pop.

family_08/archetype_058.why_selected_sources_fit: The sources combine technology background, direct synthpop style framing, and two canonical artist bridges from dark electronic pop and post-punk dance.

claims.claim_text: Synthpop moved the hook from guitar riff to keyboard line, sequenced bass, and drum-machine pattern while keeping pop-song architecture central.
Depeche Mode make the road's dark electronic-pop side audible through minor-key synth hooks, machine rhythm, and dramatic vocal presentation.
New Order are a boundary anchor because they connect post-punk austerity to club pulse and synth-led pop without becoming Chicago house.
New Romantic style and electronic pop production helped make image, fashion, and synthetic timbre part of the song's identity.

render_seed.short_definition: 1980s pop where the machine is the band and the synth line is the hook.
render_seed.history_capsule: Synthpop turned electronic instruments into mainstream emotional tools, from icy minimalism to glamorous New Romantic drama.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It normalized drum machines, sequencers, and synth timbres as pop's front line.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: Unlike house or techno, the center is usually the song, vocal, and chorus rather than the club track.
did_you_know: New Order help explain the bridge from post-punk to dance-pop.
A synthpop signal can be dark, romantic, funny, or sleek; the common thread is electronic songcraft.
render_seed.caution: Do not merge synthpop with every electronic dance style; keep verse-chorus pop form in view.

family_08/archetype_059.archetype_query: College Rock / Pre-Alternative 80s: R.E.M., The Smiths, The Replacements, Husker Du, Dinosaur Jr., college radio, jangle, literate indie guitar before mainstream alternative.

family_08/archetype_059.why_selected_sources_fit: The selected sources identify both the channel (college radio/alternative before the boom) and the anchor objects that make the sound audible.

claims.claim_text: College rock names both a sound zone and a distribution lane: independent guitar bands reaching listeners through college radio before alternative became mainstream.
R.E.M. anchor the jangly, cryptic, Southern-college side of the road, with Murmur and Radio Free Europe as clean listening doors.
The Replacements and Husker Du show the rougher branch where punk energy, melody, and damaged bar-band feeling fed later alternative rock.
This road should not be confused with grunge: it is mostly the 1980s pre-boom infrastructure that grunge and 1990s alternative later amplified.

render_seed.short_definition: The 1980s underground guitar road that alternative rock later made famous.
render_seed.history_capsule: College rock connected jangle, punk remnants, literary lyrics, and independent labels through radio stations and regional scenes.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It built the audience and values that made 1990s alternative possible.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: It is less about one sound than a family of guitar-band approaches tied by non-mainstream circulation.
did_you_know: College rock is named for a listening network, not just a musical recipe.
R.E.M. and The Replacements can both belong because the road spans polish and looseness.
render_seed.caution: Do not use college rock as a synonym for all indie; keep the 1980s pre-alternative channel central.

claims.claim_text: Noise rock and post-hardcore kept hardcore's intensity but made rhythm, dissonance, repetition, and abrasion the main expressive tools.
Fugazi anchor the post-hardcore side through tense bass/drum interplay, shouted restraint, and a clear independent-scene ethic.
The Touch and Go axis matters because it connects abrasive Midwestern and national underground guitar bands into a recognizable noisy lineage.
At the Drive-In and Slint show how this road can become theatrical, mathy, or dynamic without turning into mainstream post-grunge.

render_seed.short_definition: Hardcore after it learned angles, silence, abrasion, and architecture.
render_seed.history_capsule: This road follows loud underground guitar music after hardcore, through labels and bands that turned dissonance and dynamics into the hook.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It feeds later emo, math rock, indie noise, and heavy alternative without behaving like radio rock.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The music often feels tense and engineered from friction: bass, drums, and guitar scrape against each other.
did_you_know: Touch and Go is part of the map because labels helped define this sound's circulation.
Fugazi's restraint is as important as its volume.
render_seed.caution: Do not confuse every loud 1990s guitar band with this road; listen for underground post-hardcore structure and noise logic.

claims.claim_text: Traditional heavy metal centers the riff, amplified power, modal darkness, and dramatic vocal/guitar display, with Black Sabbath as the gravity well.
Judas Priest helped codify metal's twin-guitar attack, high-register vocals, and leather-and-studs visual grammar.
NWOBHM sharpened metal into faster, more disciplined song forms that fed Iron Maiden, thrash, and later extreme metal.
This road should be separated from hard rock by the sustained metal identity: riff weight, mythic or ominous atmosphere, and codified metal performance language.

render_seed.short_definition: The core metal language: heavy riffs, drama, power, and British codification.
render_seed.history_capsule: From Sabbath's dark heaviness to Priest and Maiden's sharpened attack, this road gives metal its central grammar.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It built the vocabulary that thrash, doom, power metal, and modern heavy music keep reusing.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The focus is not just loud rock; it is riff architecture, theatrical force, and a metal-specific identity.
did_you_know: NWOBHM is a bridge between classic heavy metal and thrash speed.
Sabbath belongs here even though they also feed doom and stoner roads.
render_seed.caution: Do not collapse traditional metal into every hard-rock band with loud guitars.

family_09/archetype_062.archetype_query: Thrash Metal / Speed Metal: Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth, Anthrax, Exodus, Testament, fast palm-muted riffs, double-time drums, 1980s metal underground.

claims.claim_text: Thrash fused NWOBHM precision with hardcore-like velocity, making palm-muted riff cycles and double-time drums the core signal.
Metallica's Master of Puppets works as an archetype anchor because it combines long-form composition with thrash speed and tightly arranged riff changes.
Slayer marks the road's darker and more extreme edge, where tempo, tremolo-like aggression, and confrontational themes point toward death and black metal gateways.
Thrash should not be confused with glam metal even when both are 1980s metal: thrash favors attack, precision, and underground credibility over glossy chorus spectacle.

render_seed.short_definition: Metal accelerated into tight, aggressive, riff-driven velocity.
render_seed.history_capsule: Thrash took traditional metal's technical force and pushed it into faster, sharper underground forms in the 1980s.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It became the major bridge from classic metal to extreme metal while still producing mainstream landmarks.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The sound is defined by riff motion, tempo, and precision more than pop hooks or blues swing.
did_you_know: The Big Four are useful survey anchors, but regional thrash scenes extend beyond them.
Thrash can be technical without losing its blunt physical attack.
render_seed.caution: Do not mistake fast hard rock for thrash unless the riffing and drum language line up.

claims.claim_text: Glam metal made heavy guitar compatible with pop choruses, image spectacle, arena scale, and power-ballad dynamics.
Def Leppard's Hysteria and Pyromania anchor the polished pop-metal side through layered production, huge drums, and precision chorus design.
Motley Crue and the Sunset Strip branch foreground sleaze, theatrical image, and party danger as much as guitar technique.
Guns N' Roses sit on the archetype boundary because Appetite for Destruction is glam-era and image-aware but rougher, bluesier, and less lacquered than pop-metal peers.

render_seed.short_definition: 1980s metal turned into neon arena pop: riffs, hooks, hair, and spectacle.
render_seed.history_capsule: Glam metal carried hard-rock and metal vocabulary into MTV-ready choruses, image theater, and enormous studio sound.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It defined a mainstream metal memory that still shapes karaoke, classic-rock radio, and power-ballad culture.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The difference is the gloss: hooks, visual identity, and chorus size are as important as riff weight.
did_you_know: Power ballads are not side notes here; they are central to the road's pop-metal function.
Guns N' Roses are useful as a boundary case, not a reason to make the whole road gritty.
render_seed.caution: Do not treat all 1980s metal as glam; separate thrash's aggression and traditional metal's codified heaviness.

render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: Instead of speed or flash, the distinct feature is mass: tone, repetition, and atmosphere carry the drama.

My Chemical Romance make the theatrical branch audible through narrative albums, dramatic vocals, punk attack, and death-glam imagery.
Fall Out Boy connect emo-pop to pop-punk and mainstream pop through dense hooks, wordplay, and rhythmically agile vocals.

render_seed.short_definition: Post-hardcore feeling turned into confession, theater, and giant 2000s hooks.
render_seed.history_capsule: This road runs from melodic emo into mall-era emo-pop, where scene identity, vulnerability, and pop structures became inseparable.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It gave a generation a dramatic language for sincerity, alienation, romance, and self-mythology.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The signal is emotional scale: tight guitars, urgent vocals, huge choruses, and often a theatrical visual world.
did_you_know: Jimmy Eat World are a gentler gateway than My Chemical Romance, but both explain the road.

Death Cab for Cutie represent the literate, melodic, emotionally restrained branch that connected indie rooms to mainstream listeners.
Modest Mouse and The National show the road's range from nervy existential guitar pop to baritone adult melancholy, so the archetype should not be reduced to one production sound.

render_seed.short_definition: 2000s indie rock as canon culture: blogs, festivals, labels, and emotionally ambitious albums.
render_seed.history_capsule: This road captures the moment indie became a prestige language, from communal orchestral catharsis to literate guitar melancholy.

did_you_know: Pitchfork-era attention helped turn some indie records into instant reference points.

The Strokes' Is This It anchors the New York side through dry vocals, clipped riffs, compressed cool, and songs that sound casual but are tightly designed.
The White Stripes anchor the raw blues-garage branch, proving the revival could feel primitive, theatrical, and massive with minimal instrumentation.
Yeah Yeah Yeahs and The Hives sit near the boundary with post-punk revival and punk showmanship, so the garage signal should stay tied to stripped riff economy.

render_seed.short_definition: The early-2000s 'rock is back' lane: lean guitars, vintage attitude, and controlled rawness.
render_seed.history_capsule: Garage revival made small, sharp guitar bands feel urgent again after nu-metal, post-grunge, and electronic gloss dominated the edges of rock culture.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It reset indie-rock style for the 2000s and gave guitar minimalism a new mass memory.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The signal is deliberate reduction: fewer parts, cooler surfaces, tighter riffs, and retro electricity.
did_you_know: The Strokes and White Stripes are complementary rather than identical anchors.
The phrase 'rock is back' was media shorthand for a broader early-2000s guitar revival.
render_seed.caution: Do not use garage revival for every 2000s indie band; keep the stripped retro guitar language central.

Interpol anchor the dark indie side through baritone vocals, monochrome atmosphere, precise basslines, and controlled guitar tension.
Franz Ferdinand show the dance-rock branch where jagged guitar and disco-punk rhythm make post-punk revival feel bright and kinetic.
Yeah Yeah Yeahs belong near the garage revival boundary, but Maps and Fever to Tell also carry art-punk drama and dark indie intensity.

render_seed.short_definition: 2000s indie rediscovering post-punk's angles, basslines, and dark dance-floor tension.
render_seed.history_capsule: This road follows bands that made older post-punk moves feel new inside the blog/indie era: sharp guitars, cool surfaces, and rhythm you can dance to.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It helped define 2000s indie style alongside garage revival and dance-punk.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: The distinction is angularity and mood: darker, more bass-driven, and more mannered than simple garage rock revival.
did_you_know: Interpol and Franz Ferdinand prove the road can be dark or bright while still post-punk-revival coded.
Yeah Yeah Yeahs are a useful boundary because they touch garage, art-punk, and dark indie.

claims.claim_text: Chicago house grew from DJ-centered club culture, especially extended dance-floor practice that reworked disco, soul, and electronic rhythm into track-based form.
Frankie Knuckles is a central anchor because his Warehouse-era DJ practice and later productions connect the archetype's club, community, and recording histories.
The listening clues are steady four-on-the-floor kick, repeating bassline, piano or synth stabs, soulful vocal fragments, and gradual dance-floor build.
Acid house and early Trax-style records sit inside the broader house foundation because cheap machines made hypnotic local club tracks portable worldwide.

render_seed.short_definition: Chicago club foundations: soulful repetition, machines, DJs, and dancers building the track together.
render_seed.history_capsule: House emerged from Chicago dance spaces where DJs, drum machines, disco memory, queer nightlife, and Black/Latino club culture made a new electronic pulse.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It rewired global pop and club music around the producer/DJ and the repeating groove.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: Unlike techno's colder futurism, house keeps a warmer relationship to disco, soul, vocals, and communal release.
did_you_know: Frankie Knuckles is called a foundational figure because the DJ booth and the studio both matter to house history.
Acid house is a machine mutation inside house's wider Chicago story.

claims.claim_text: Detroit techno developed as a futurist electronic dance language built from drum machines, synthesizers, sequencers, and the city's post-industrial imagination.
Juan Atkins and Cybotron/Model 500 anchor the road because they connect electro, futurism, and stripped machine funk to techno's early identity.
Kevin Saunderson shows the bridge from Detroit techno's machine logic to more songful, club-accessible dance records without leaving the Detroit frame.
Underground Resistance marks the archetype's political and underground branch, where label identity, anonymity, and Detroit futurism matter as much as track structure.

render_seed.short_definition: Detroit machine futurism: precise pulse, synthetic space, and underground imagination.
render_seed.history_capsule: Techno emerged in Detroit as electronic dance music that treated machines as vehicles for futurism, repetition, and post-industrial feeling.
render_seed.why_it_mattered: It gave global club culture a new template for producer identity, minimal structure, and machine emotion.
render_seed.what_made_it_distinct: Compared with Chicago house, techno is usually cooler, more synthetic, more futurist, and more rhythmically architectural.
did_you_know: The Belleville Three shorthand points to Juan Atkins, Derrick May, and Kevin Saunderson, but Detroit techno extends beyond that trio.
Underground Resistance makes the political and label-infrastructure side audible.

Portishead make the noir branch audible through spy-film guitar, turntable texture, haunted vocals, and breakbeats that feel suspended in smoke.
DJ Shadow and Tricky widen the road toward instrumental sample collage and darker vocal/persona experiments without turning it into festival dance music.

render_seed.history_capsule: Trip-hop and downtempo emerged around Bristol and adjacent sample culture by slowing the dance impulse into mood, shadow, and groove.
